chunks: Vias between inner layers. The question: If I need to via between inner layers, what type of vias would I use?
To connect two inner layers of a board, you use a buried via. It lives entirely inside the board and never shows on the top or bottom.
The board factory (fab) drills and plates it in a thin inner core before the board is pressed together. That extra build step makes it cost more.
In return it takes no space on the outer layers and leaves no stub.
Picture a staircase between two middle floors of a building. It does not reach the street or the roof, so it uses no ground-floor or roof space.
But it has to be built before the upper floors go on, and afterward you cannot see or repair it. A stairwell through every floor is simpler, but it cuts a hole in every floor.
The shaded centre core carries L3 and L4. The buried via is drilled and plated in that core alone, before the outer layers are laminated onto it, so its barrel is only 0.
2 mm long. The through via on the right spans all six layers and goes through the plane layers with antipads.
Buried via: a plated hole that connects inner layers only. Core: a thin insulating sheet with copper on both sides. It is the building block of the board.
Lamination: pressing the layers together with heat to form the finished board. Through via: a hole through the whole board. It touches every layer.
Stub: the unused part of a through via barrel, which can disturb fast signals. Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast current changes.
Say you need to connect inner layers 3 and 4 of a six-layer board. A through via would run 1. 6 mm through all six layers, cut holes in both ground planes, and leave stubs.
Its inductance is about 1. 3 nanohenries, which at 5 gigahertz acts like about 41 ohms. A buried via in a 0. 2 mm core is only 0. 2 mm long. Its inductance is about 0.
1 nanohenries, 13 times lower, or about 3 ohms at 5 gigahertz, and it has no stub.
That is the whole idea: build the short connection inside the board, at the price of extra manufacturing steps.
"I'd use a buried via. It connects two inner layers, never reaches the surface, and is drilled and plated in a core before the final lamination.
That saves outer-layer space and avoids a stub, but it needs sequential lamination, so it costs more and can't be inspected or reworked.
If density or signal integrity doesn't justify it, a through via, possibly back-drilled, is the cheaper alternative."
